lead: Mass transfer is easier to write once every species has its own velocity. Species A moves with velocity v_A, and c_A v_A is its molar flux N_A. That flux contains two parts: A drifting relative to the mixture, and the whole mixture moving. This chapter fixes the vocabulary of velocities, fluxes and reference frames for binary and multicomponent mixtures. It also separates molecular diffusion, the random walk of molecules, from eddy diffusion, the mixing by turbulent lumps. Every later calculation of D, absorption and distillation uses this language.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for concentration, mole fraction and the idea of a component moving because of a concentration difference.

blocks.text: Pick a small window fixed to the laboratory wall. Species i crosses it with an average velocity v_i, in m/s. Its molar concentration is c_i, in mol/m³. The molar flux of i through this fixed window is N_i = c_i v_i, in mol/(m²·s). The total concentration is c = Σc_i, and the mole fraction is y_i = c_i/c. For a binary mixture A + B, c = c_A + c_B and y_A + y_B = 1.

The molar flux N_A is not the mass flux. The mass flux is n_A = ρ_A v_A = M_A N_A, in kg/(m²·s). Here ρ_A is the mass concentration in kg/m³ and M_A is the molar mass in kg/mol. The mass fraction is w_A = ρ_A/ρ. Use the table to keep the objects separate.

sections.h3: Molar average velocity and diffusion flux

blocks.text: The mixture itself has a velocity. The molar average velocity is u = Σc_i v_i/c = ΣN_i/c, in m/s. For a binary, u = (N_A + N_B)/c. The diffusion velocity of A is v_A − u. The diffusion flux of A is J_A = c_A(v_A − u), in mol/(m²·s). This J_A is measured relative to the molar-average frame, not the laboratory wall.

Add and subtract c_A u: N_A = c_A v_A = c_A u + c_A(v_A − u) = y_A(N_A + N_B) + J_A. Rearranged, N_A = J_A + y_A(N_A + N_B). The term y_A(N_A + N_B) is the bulk flow; it is not diffusion. In a binary, J_A = −J_B because c_A(v_A − u) + c_B(v_B − u) = Σc_i v_i − c u = 0. But N_A is not −N_B unless the fluxes are equimolar, N_A + N_B = 0.

blocks.where: N_A and N_B are fixed-frame molar fluxes in mol/(m²·s); J_A is the diffusion flux of A in mol/(m²·s); y_A is the mole fraction of A. The second term is the bulk flow.

blocks.text: Other frames have other names. The mass-average velocity is u_m = Σρ_i v_i/ρ, and the mass-average diffusion flux is j_A = ρ_A(v_A − u_m). The volume-average frame uses volume-fraction weighting; it is common for liquid mixtures. Use N_A in the fixed frame, J_A in the molar-average frame, and j_A in the mass-average frame.

Molecular diffusion comes from random molecular motion. Molecules of A and B collide and swap places even when the fluid is still. Eddy diffusion comes from turbulence. Eddies carry lumps of fluid, with their A and B, from one place to another. Eddy diffusion is fast in the core of a pipe and zero at a solid wall, where the eddy size falls to zero.

The measured mean flux can contain both parts. Write J_A = J_A(mol) + J_A(eddy), then N_A = J_A + y_A(N_A + N_B). The eddy part is modelled with an eddy diffusivity D_E, in m²/s: J_A(eddy) = −D_E dc_A/dz. Here dc_A/dz is the gradient of the mean concentration, in mol/m⁴. D_E depends on flow speed, geometry and distance from the wall; it is not a property of the A–B pair. At the wall D_E → 0, so only molecular diffusion survives.

The molecular part uses D_AB, the molecular diffusivity of the pair at that temperature and pressure. Chapter 1.3 gives Fick's law for that part. Unit 2 turns the near-wall molecular region into a mass transfer coefficient. For a dilute species, engineers often add D_AB + D_E as an effective diffusivity, but the bulk term stays separate.

spec.title: From species velocity to total flux

examples.question: A binary gas at 300 K and 1 atm has c = 40.6 mol/m³ and y_A = 0.30. The measured molar fluxes are N_A = 3.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s) and N_B = 1.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s). Find the molar average velocity u, the diffusion flux J_A, the velocity of A and its diffusion velocity.
steps: Given c = 40.6 mol/m³, y_A = 0.30, N_A = 3.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s), N_B = 1.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s). The total molar flux is N_A + N_B = 4.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s).
Molar average velocity: u = (N_A + N_B)/c = 4.0×10⁻³/40.6 = 9.85×10⁻⁵ m/s.
Concentration of A: c_A = y_A c = 0.30 × 40.6 = 12.18 mol/m³.
Velocity of A: v_A = N_A/c_A = 3.0×10⁻³/12.18 = 2.46×10⁻⁴ m/s.
examples.answer: u = 9.85×10⁻⁵ m/s, J_A = 1.8×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s), c_A = 12.18 mol/m³, v_A = 2.46×10⁻⁴ m/s, and the diffusion velocity v_A − u = 1.48×10⁻⁴ m/s.
examples.check:
c = 40.6
yA = 0.30
NA = 3.0e-3
NB = 1.0e-3
Ntot = NA + NB
u = Ntot / c
cA = yA * c
JA = NA - yA * Ntot
vA = NA / cA
vdiff = vA - u
print(f'{u:.2e}')
print(f'{JA:.1e}')
print(f'{cA:.2f}')
print(f'{vA:.2e}')
print(f'{vdiff:.2e}')

traps: Calling N_A the diffusion flux. N_A is the fixed-frame flux; J_A is the diffusion flux. At large y_A the bulk term y_A(N_A + N_B) is a big part of N_A. Setting N_A = J_A gives a wrong D in Chapter 1.3.
Assuming N_A = −N_B always. Only equimolar counter-diffusion has that; in general J_A = −J_B while N_A + N_B is not zero.
Mixing units of mass and molar flux. n_A = M_A N_A; use kg/(m²·s) for n_A and mol/(m²·s) for N_A.
Using the molar average velocity u as the fluid flow velocity. u is a concentration-weighted mean of species velocities; the bulk term is y_A(N_A + N_B), not c_A times a guessed flow.
Treating eddy diffusivity D_E as a fluid property. D_E depends on turbulence and position and falls to zero at a wall; D_AB depends on the pair, temperature and pressure.

quiz.q: Define the molar flux N_A and the diffusion flux J_A. State the frame and SI unit of each.
quiz.a: N_A = c_A v_A is the molar flux of A through the fixed laboratory frame, in mol/(m²·s). J_A = c_A(v_A − u) is the diffusion flux relative to the molar-average frame, also in mol/(m²·s).

quiz.q: In a binary mixture, why is J_A = −J_B but N_A usually not −N_B?
quiz.a: By definition, J_A + J_B = c_A(v_A − u) + c_B(v_B − u) = Σc_i v_i − c u = 0, so J_A = −J_B. The total fluxes are N_A = J_A + y_A(N_A + N_B) and N_B = J_B + y_B(N_A + N_B); their sum is the bulk flow, which is zero only for equimolar counter-diffusion.

quiz.q: A binary gas has c = 50 mol/m³, y_A = 0.20, N_A = 4.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s) and N_B = 1.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s). Find u, c_A, J_A and v_A.
A student sets N_A = J_A for a concentrated binary gas. Explain the error and its effect on the diffusivity found from the next chapter.
quiz.a: N_A includes the bulk term y_A(N_A + N_B), which is large when y_A is large. Setting N_A = J_A drops this term and misreads the diffusion driving force. Fick's law then gives a D that is too small or too large depending on the flow direction; the error grows as y_A approaches 1.

quiz.q: Distinguish molecular diffusion from eddy diffusion. Why does eddy diffusivity fall to zero at a solid wall?
quiz.a: Molecular diffusion is random molecular motion and exists even in a still fluid. Eddy diffusion is mixing by turbulent eddies carrying fluid lumps. At a wall the turbulent fluctuations are suppressed, so eddy size and D_E fall to zero; only molecular diffusion remains.

quiz.q: The molar flux of A is 0.002 mol/(m²·s) and its molar mass is 0.044 kg/mol. Find the mass flux n_A.
Write the relation between total molar flux and diffusion flux for a binary mixture. Name the bulk-flow term.
quiz.a: N_A = J_A + y_A(N_A + N_B). The term y_A(N_A + N_B) is the bulk-flow contribution.

beyond: Not for the exam. In CFD, the eddy diffusivity is supplied by turbulence models such as k–ε or k–ω, and the mass flux is closed with a turbulent Schmidt number. In microfluidics the same split matters because the bulk term can dominate when two streams merge. Membrane boundary layers use the film model, which is a mass transfer coefficient version of this chapter. Search next for turbulent Schmidt number, eddy diffusivity, and Stefan–Maxwell equations.
